articles.title: Mojtaba Khamenei defies ‘malicious’ attacks as US Army zeroes in on Iran’s 350,000 troops
articles.summary: Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei claimed U.S. and Israeli strikes failed to weaken Iran's military, as the U.S. Army released a new threat guide.
articles.body: Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei claimed Oct. 8 that U.S. and Israeli strikes had failed to undermine Iran's domestic security forces, praising police personnel for resisting attacks launched in February under Operations Epic Fury and Roaring Lion. Khamenei's remarks on X also came as the U.S. Army released a new battlefield identification guide to help American troops recognize members of Iran's conventional military, known as the Artesh, whose ground forces were estimated by the Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security in June at 350,000 personnel. "The criminal US-Zionist enemy's desperate efforts and malicious attacks on the pillars of social order and security, which are unparalleled throughout history, have not caused the courageous personnel of the Police Force to waver even a fraction in their mission," Khamenei wrote in a statement. Khamenei specifically praised Iran's Law Enforcement Command, known as FARAJA, accusing the United States and Israel of targeting the institution responsible for maintaining domestic order. "The focus and persistence of the criminal US-Zionist enemy in striking at the Police Force at its various levels, from its highest command levels down to those who are on the frontline, has only served to underscore the paramount importance of this institution more than ever," he wrote. IRAN PROVES THAT IT MIGHT CHANGE ITS MILITARY LEADERS, BUT IT’S NOT CHANGING STRATEGY Iran's security apparatus comprises three principal branches: the Artesh, responsible primarily for conventional territorial defense; the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), tasked with protecting the Islamic Republic and projecting military power; and FARAJA, responsible for domestic law enforcement and internal security. IRAN’S GUTTED RANKS LEAVE LOYALISTS FILLING CRITICAL POSTS — WITH ONE GLARING PROBLEM FARAJA, commanded by Brig. Gen. Ahmadreza Radan, is responsible for maintaining public order, enforcing the country's laws and responding to civil unrest. According to Iran Human Rights Monitor, the force has evolved into a powerful internal security institution involved in suppressing anti-government demonstrations, monitoring political activity and enforcing the regime's ideological restrictions. IRAN INSTALLS NEW WAR CHIEFS AS TEHRAN SIGNALS ‘PROLONGED CONFRONTATION,’ EXPERT WARNS Radan has also been sanctioned by the United States for his role in human rights abuses. The Treasury Department designated him in September 2010, citing his responsibility for beatings, killings and arbitrary arrests of protesters following Iran's disputed 2009 presidential election. Khamenei also called for strengthening FARAJA on Oct. 8 through additional personnel, equipment and technology, including the use of artificial intelligence for data analysis. AFTER 47 YEARS OF CONFRONTING IRAN, DOES AMERICA HAVE A STRATEGY FOR ENDING THIS WAR? His remarks come as the U.S. Army's Training and Transformation Command published a "Know the Threat" recognition guide Sept. 24, highlighted by Defense News on Oct. 9. The guide shows an Iranian special forces soldier and identifies weapons American troops could encounter, including AKM rifles, Iranian-made Masaf-2 rifles, German-designed G3 rifles, MG3 machine guns and RPG-7 rocket-propelled grenade launchers. The Artesh, Iran's regular military, is separate from the IRGC and its affiliated Basij militia. Its forces operate across four branches: the Ground Forces, Navy, Air Force and Air Defense Force. A June assessment by the Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security estimated the Artesh's Ground Forces at approximately 350,000 personnel, including 220,000 conscripts. The report found that the Artesh had suffered severe losses across its air, naval and air defense components during the opening phase of the U.S.-Israeli military campaign, while its ground forces remained structurally intact because there had been no ground invasion. TRUMP OPENS HORMUZ UNDER FIRE WITH ‘PROJECT FREEDOM’ AS IRAN WARNS OF ATTACKS The Artesh is commanded by Maj. Gen. Amir Hatami, a former Iranian defense minister who assumed command in June 2025. Aside from Khamenei, Hatami issued his own warning Oct. 6, claiming Iran's adversaries faced "historic confusion" after failing to halt military production during the conflict. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Hatami also claimed that Iranian defense production continued despite American and Israeli attacks, saying the country's military production lines had continued operating during the conflict. The extent of Iran's military recovery remains unclear. The Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security assessed in June that the country's conventional air, naval and air defense forces had suffered severe damage during the conflict. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, said Oct. 8 that Washington would not resume military strikes against Iran before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, citing "productive discussions" between the two countries.

articles.title: Toddler stabbed in face, suspect previously deemed unfit for trial in attacks on 2 children: report
articles.summary: Nelson Blanco allegedly stabbed a toddler at a Rhode Island school bus stop, decades after being found incompetent to stand trial for knifing two boys.
articles.body: A stranger allegedly stabbed a toddler in the face as she sat in her stroller at a Rhode Island school bus stop, years after he was accused of knifing two other children and found incompetent to stand trial. The child’s fight for survival has brought renewed scrutiny into the suspect’s past, including an attack on two children more than two decades ago and repeated findings that he was incompetent to stand trial. Nelson Blanco, 46, is accused of stabbing the 2-year-old girl and her mother Wednesday afternoon near Broad and Public streets in Providence, police said. SOUTH CAROLINA MOM ACCUSED OF KNIFE ATTACK ON YOUNG CHILDREN; 6-YEAR-OLD MAY LOSE ARM: SHERIFF'S OFFICE The toddler was taken to Hasbro Children’s Hospital in critical condition. Her mother, who suffered a stab wound to the shoulder, was treated and released, according to local reporting. The mother was waiting with her daughter for her other children to get off a school bus when Blanco allegedly approached and made insulting comments, Providence Police Chief Oscar Perez said, according to WPRI. ANGEL MOM SAYS BLUE STATE DAS ARE PUTTING ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CRIMINALS BEFORE PUBLIC SAFETY She crossed the street with the stroller to get away, but Blanco approached again and allegedly attacked the child with a knife, police said, noting there was no evidence he knew either victim. Surveillance video showed the mother and daughter attempting to move away before Blanco grabbed the stroller and struck the child repeatedly, Boston 25 News reported. A bystander tried to intervene, but Blanco allegedly attempted to stab that person before fleeing, according to the outlet. Officers found Blanco hiding in the basement of a nearby home and recovered a knife from a panel box, police said. Authorities said he admitted to the stabbings during questioning. CALIFORNIA STABBING VICTIM'S FRIEND BLASTS 'FAILED' JUSTICE SYSTEM OVER ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT SUSPECT'S RELEASE Blanco allegedly told detectives he stopped the attack because he was on a main street, according to a police report obtained by WPRI. "If I was on a side street, I would have killed them. Both of them," he said, according to the outlet. PROSECUTORS SAY CHARLOTTE TRAIN STABBING CASE WON'T BE DISMISSED REGARDLESS OF COMPETENCY RULING Blanco faces six charges, including two counts police identified as assault with intent to commit murder, felony assault, breaking and entering into an occupied dwelling of a person 60 or older, and two weapons charges. No plea was entered during his Thursday appearance in Rhode Island’s 6th Division District Court. The court referred him to the public defender and requested an evaluation, according to court records reviewed by Fox News Digital. VIOLENT TRANSIT ATTACKS IN ATLANTA, NEW YORK AND CHARLOTTE FUEL CALLS FOR TOUGHER TRACKING OF REPEAT OFFENDERS WPRI reported Blanco is being held without bail pending a competency hearing later this month. His arrest brought back painful memories for Andy Lopez and Dave Belony, who told WPRI they were 6 and 7 years old when Blanco attacked them while they played in Lopez’s backyard on Sept. 27, 2003. CHARLOTTE REPEAT OFFENDER CHARGED WITH KILLING MAN HOURS AFTER RELEASE ON BOND Belony said he recognized Blanco immediately when he saw his booking photo on social media Wednesday night. "I knew it was him, because I will always remember that face," he told the station. "My heart dropped, and it truly felt like my world had stopped." Court records reviewed by Fox News Digital show Blanco faced two felony assault charges and a charge of possessing a knife or firearm during a crime, stemming from the 2003 incident. BANK OF AMERICA EXEC KILLED IN RANDOM TIMES SQUARE STABBING LAID TO REST AS HUNDREDS MOURN YOUNG MOM The docket documents repeated findings that Blanco was incompetent to stand trial from September 2004 through March 2006. Multiple entries state, "Defendant Remains Incompetent." The case remains listed as "under review" in the court portal. More recently, Blanco was found incompetent to stand trial in July in a separate domestic violence case, WPRI reported. A judge accepted a doctor’s recommendation allowing him to remain in outpatient treatment because he was considered unlikely to endanger the community or himself at that time. Lopez and Belony said the earlier attack left them with injuries and trauma that have followed them into adulthood. They told WPRI they were playing with Lopez’s brother when Blanco emerged from a shed behind the house where he had been living. "He didn’t say a word," Belony recalled. "His face was blank and he was just staring at us." Belony said Blanco charged at him, trapping him near a tree. He curled into a ball and covered his head as Blanco stabbed him. DEMOCRATIC BOSTON COUNCILOR RIPS 'SOFT-ON-CRIME' POLICIES AFTER SUSPECTED GUNMAN'S VIOLENT PAST REVEALED Blanco then turned toward Lopez, the men said. "My brother yelled at me to run, and I was trying to run but my body just froze," Lopez told WPRI. "He stabbed me twice in the eye — the first time it was blurry, and then the second time I couldn’t see anything." Both children were rushed to Hasbro Children’s Hospital. Their recovery took three months and included at least three surgeries each, they told the outlet. Lopez was left permanently blind in his left eye, an injury he said derailed his dreams of becoming a police officer or truck driver. "Most of the opportunities I wanted to have in life are gone," he said. "I’m very grateful I’m alive, but my life is restricted." Belony said he was stabbed at least five times in his stomach, back and ribs and continues to struggle emotionally. The men said learning about the latest attack left them devastated for the mother and toddler, and determined to speak out. "It’s frustrating for us, not only because of what happened to us, but because it has happened to others," Lopez told WPRI. "He was given a chance 23 years ago, and 23 years later, he did the same thing." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "We want justice for the victims," Belony said. "What is it going to take for him to be held accountable for his actions?" Fox News Digital reached out to the Providence Police Department and the Rhode Island attorney general’s office for comment.

articles.title: Two killed near Israeli-occupied area in south Lebanon
articles.summary: Despite ceasefire reached between Israel and Lebanon in June, Israeli attacks continue.
articles.body:
Two men have been killed in southern Lebanon’s Bint Jbeil district while taking part in an annual olive harvest, according to Lebanese state media and local authorities, as attacks by Israel continue.

One of the men died Sunday in the village of Froun from a munition left behind by recent fighting and the other in Yater as a result of Israeli shelling that “targeted the outskirts of the town while he was inspecting his land and olive harvest”, according to the official National News Agency (NNA).

The Lebanese army blamed Israeli tank fire and called the ongoing attacks “a flagrant breach of existing agreements”.

Afterwards, the Yater municipality urged residents “to avoid the outskirts of the town and refrain from crossing the earthen barrier separating some unsafe neighbourhoods” for fear of Israeli attacks.

In Froun, the NNA reported that “a foreign object” left over from previous Israeli operations exploded and killed the man, who was an engineer, as he and others tended their trees.

The engineer had come down from Beirut, where he lives, for the harvest, Froun mayor Hassan Bazzi told AFP.

The incident prompted local residents to call off the harvest and wait for “the Lebanese army to complete the decontamination of the village”, Bazzi said.

Since an agreement between Lebanon and Israel was struck in June, violence in the south has lessened, but not stopped .

Lebanon was pulled into conflict on March 2, when Hezbollah struck Israel in support of Tehran during the US-Israel war on Iran. Subsequently, Israel launched a bombing campaign and a ground invasion that authorities say have killed more than 4,300.

In August, Lebanon’s Prime Minister Nawaf Salam accused Israel of intentionally targeting homes and civilian infrastructure across the country. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) recorded nearly 350,000 internally displaced people in late August, a sign of the worsening displacement crisis.

Volunteers from the nearby town of Jebchit and locals came to help their southern neighbours with the harvest in an act of solidarity.

“From north to south, one people and one land,” said organiser Ahmad Chahhal.

articles.title: 'Prepare for the unthinkable' warning over autumn flooding forecast
articles.summary: Those living in flood-hit areas say they are worried, and have started preparing.
articles.body:
People are being told to prepare for "the unthinkable" as flood response teams warn of a heightened risk over the autumn.

Natural Resources Wales (NRW) said it was concerned by long-range forecasts which indicated an increased likelihood of wetter, windier weather than usual over the coming months.

Those living in flood-hit areas told BBC Wales they were worried, and had started preparing.

One in seven properties in Wales is classed as being at risk of flooding, but NRW said just 27% of those eligible to receive flood warnings to their phone or email were currently signed up.

After a summer marked by drought and wildfires , the organisation has urged people "not to become complacent" and said conditions could change quickly.

Wales has seen a series of major floods in recent years, often in the wake of powerful storms such as Dennis in 2020 , Bert and Darragh in 2024 and Claudia in 2025 .

The threat comes from both rivers and the sea, while surface water flooding - where local drainage systems become overwhelmed during heavy downpours - is seen as an increasing danger.

NRW argues that the country's geography makes it particularly vulnerable - with a vast coastline and several so-called "fast-responding" rivers which can fill at speed as rain runs off steep terrain in places like the south Wales valleys.

More than 274,500 homes and businesses are currently classed at risk of flooding, with this figure set to increase significantly by the end of the century.

On the high street in Monmouth, people told BBC Wales of "harrowing" and "dreadful" scenes when major flooding hit in November 2025.

Friends Malcolm Butcher, 82, Jim Tyler, 81, Brian Churches, 82 and Dave Blake, 82, said they had lived in the town all their lives "and never seen anything like it".

"At 2:30 in the morning when it hit it was unbelievable... absolutely raging," Malcolm said.

If it had happened in the daytime "people would have died", he added.

Eighteen cars on his road were lost to the flood waters - including his own, while the houses in the street behind were all flooded out.

"It is a worry, we have three rivers running into Monmouth... and the winters are changing," he said.

People could help prepare for floods by moving "the good stuff upstairs" and making sure they had sandbags to hand ahead of bad weather, he said.

"It's not back to normal yet but we're getting there," added Imogen Elliot, 82.

"Waitrose was four feet in water and it went right up the street - we've had flooding before but not like that."

Jane Roche, who runs a café and fishmongers on the banks of the River Teifi in Cardigan, Ceredigion, has helped coordinate a community flood plan for the area.

"Flooding is something we've learned to live alongside for many years - we've seen first-hand the disruption it can cause for businesses, residents and visitors," she said.

"Developing a community flood plan has brought local people together, helped us understand what actions we need to taken when warnings are issued and given us confidence to support one another when severe weather is forecast."

More frequent and intense weather extremes are expected as a result of climate change, with Wales facing the prospect of wetter, wilder winters more often.

Meanwhile, this year scientists are monitoring the El Niño event over the Pacific Ocean - which set to be "strongest in living memory".

The powerful natural climate phenomenon pushes up global temperatures and can increase the risks of extreme weather.

While this does not automatically translate into bad weather in the UK it is "part of the picture" that is leading to concerns for the coming months, according to Jeremy Parr of NRW.

"We do invest in flood defences... but you can't stop all of the flooding all of the time," he said.

"So that means that people need to think the unthinkable really - or the unpleasant - and [consider] if it were to flood around where I live, what would I do?"

"Time and time again" the organisation was told by people who had experienced devastating flooding that "they'd never flooded before, and didn't think it would happen to them", he added.

NRW advises people to check their flood risk by postcode online , sign up for flood warnings and access advice about what to do if flooding is forecast in their area.

The organisation's flood warning service is available to 181,158 properties in Wales, but new figures show just 48,844 were currently signed up to receive the alerts via phone or email.

"It is low - 27%," Parr admitted, suggesting that people may be being put off by myths that signing up could affect their insurance premiums.

Cardigan's mayor Olwen Davies has bought a flood door for her own house, and also uses a flood gate for extra protection.

She said: "The river comes up once or twice a year... if there's a high tide, with a strong south-westerly wind that's what creates the most havoc.

"We work together and we know who to call on," she said.

Sarah Davies from the Met Office said long-range forecasts for October, November and December suggested "a greater chance of weather-related disruption".

"Weather patterns can change quickly at this time of year, and long-range forecasts describe broad seasonal trends rather than the timing, location and severity of individual weather events," she added.

"Whatever the season, understanding your flood risk and knowing what action to take if warnings are issued are sensible steps that can help you prepare should severe weather occur."

articles.title: Lane Kiffin is staring down disastrous year one as offseason pleas for patience fall on deaf ears
articles.summary: Lane Kiffin's $40 million LSU Tigers roster faces mounting pressure after a stunning 35-34 loss to Will Stein's Kentucky Wildcats at Kroger Field.
articles.body: One of the biggest, most consequential games of the season so far took place in Tuscaloosa on Saturday night — in the wake of a hurricane, no less — but a different game was taking place about six hours north on I-65 that was also rife with national implications. The Kentucky Wildcats and LSU Tigers played an all-time classic of a college football game this weekend, with Big Blue Nation pulling off a stunner, downing the top-ten Tigers 35-34 in front of a sold-out crowd at Kroger Field. What this means for the Wildcats and first-year head coach Will Stein can't be overstated, as the new Kentucky head man now has two top-ten wins in his first six games on the job, and the arrow is pointing straight up in the Bluegrass State as of mid-October. KENTUCKY COACH WILL STEIN TELLS WILDCATS PLAYERS 'IF YOU DON'T BELIEVE IN WHAT WE'RE DOING, YOU ARE HIGH' But on the opposite sideline on Saturday night, LSU head coach Lane Kiffin was left with more questions than answers as the honeymoon phase in Baton Rouge likely came to a screeching halt. Things aren't exactly up in smoke for Kiffin in his first year on the Bayou. LANE KIFFIN KNOWS THERE AREN’T EXCUSES AT LSU. NOW COMES THE TEST OF MAKING IT WORTH THE PRICE OF ADMISSION The Tigers are 4-2 with wins over Clemson and Texas A&M and are still in the AP top-25 as of this afternoon, falling from 10th to 22nd. However, this probably isn't how anyone in purple and gold expected the season to go when they imagined the infinite possibilities back in August. LSU had one of the most expensive rosters in the country, estimated at around $40 million, as well as a coaching staff many considered to be the best in the country, top to bottom. The loss to Ole Miss three weeks ago stung, but was not unexpected. The Rebels were favored and had the benefit of playing at home, and the added context of Kiffin returning to the program, he turned his back on to go coach in The Boot made that a tough one to win. But losing to a first-time head coach at a program that you have a marked talent and resources advantage over is a tough pill to swallow. WHO'S REALLY PLAYED THE BEST THUS FAR THROUGH THE FIRST HALF OF THE COLLEGE FOOTBALL SEASON? And to top it all off, the Tigers took a massive L on the recruiting trail on Sunday when their flip target, five-star wide receiver and former Texas commit Easton Royal, opted to head to Gainesville and play for the Gators. Losing a five-star prospect to an in-conference rival is never fun, but when you consider Royal is from nearby New Orleans and was long thought to be an LSU lean even while committed to the Longhorns, it makes it even harder to accept. Sure, signing day is still two months away, but that's a prospect you'd rather hold onto than try to flip in the 11th hour. Things don't get any easier for the Bayou Bengals, either. Their October features a visit from top-20 Mississippi State as well as a trip to Jordan Hare to play Auburn. Then they play three consecutive top-15 teams in November (Alabama, Texas, and at Tennessee) before a relative break on the road against Arkansas to end the season. It's not inconceivable to envision another two losses in that stretch. If you asked an LSU fan over the summer if 8-4 was an acceptable year one, they would have laughed in your face, and they would have had every right to do so. Between Kiffin, the coaching staff, and the roster, this is easily a $150 million operation, and 8-4 and a trip to the Duke's Mayo Bowl isn't going to cut the mustard. Kiffin famously pleaded for patience during spring practice, but unfortunately for him, in this day and age of NIL and the transfer portal, patience no longer exists at a tier one program like LSU. My confidence in Kiffin's ability to win at LSU has not waned. First years are rife with trial and error, and not every coach can have a Curt Cignetti-type start to their tenure. Kiffin and his staff will figure out what works and what doesn't on this roster, and trim the fat where necessary. As long as the powers that be continue to fund this thing, LSU and Kiffin will be fine. But Saturday night's loss to Kentucky raises those same uncomfortable questions I already discussed. Why couldn't a $40 million roster and one of the hottest coaches in the country beat a lower-tier SEC team. If Will Stein can do it in year one, why can't Lane Kiffin? I'm not here to answer those questions or even argue their validity, but this is what folks in Baton Rouge will no doubt be thinking this week. articles.title: Gavin and Stacey's Melanie Walters voted off Strictly Coming Dancing
articles.summary: Walters, best known for playing Gwen West in the BBC comedy, was partnered with professional Aljaz Skorjanec.
articles.body:
Gavin and Stacey's Melanie Walters has become the second celebrity eliminated from this season of Strictly Come Dancing.

The actress, 64, had been paired with professional dancer Aljaz Skorjanec, 36.

On Saturday night's episode, Walters and Skorjanec had performed a Charleston to Ooh Ahh… Just A Little Bit by Gina G, receiving a score of 17 from the judges.

Judge Craig Revel Horwood said he "didn't love" their dance while Motsi Mabuse encouraged her to "keep going".

After finishing in the bottom two on the first two weeks of the competition, the judges sent the pair home.

On Sunday night's results episode, they were sent into the dance-off against former footballer Shaun Wright-Phillips and his partner Alexis Warr, who had received a score of 15 for their quickstep to I'm A Believer by The Monkees.

After both couples performed their routines again, the judges delivered their verdicts on who they wanted to save.

While Mabuse wanted to save Walters, fellow judges Shirley Ballas, Anton Du Beke and Revel Horwood all chose to save Wright-Phillips and Warr.

The eliminated couple will appear on It Takes Two on Monday.

articles.title: Washington's historic East Potomac golf course could lose up to 529 trees, with 169 slated for removal starting October 10; officials call it maintenance as a lawsuit challenges the park's possible redesign
articles.summary: Washington’s historic East Potomac Golf Links is facing another round of tree removals as the Trump administration weighs a potential overhaul of the
articles.body: Washington’s historic East Potomac Golf Links is facing another round of tree removals as the Trump administration weighs a potential overhaul of the century-old public golf course. According to reporting by The Washington Post and Axios, the National Park Service (NPS) has defended the clearing as maintenance, even as preservationists and park users question whether the work could pave the way for a larger redevelopment. In a court filing reported on October 9, the government disclosed plans to remove 169 trees in the first phase of the latest operation, followed by another 90 in a subsequent phase. The total number of trees potentially affected could reach 529, adding to the removals that have already drawn public scrutiny.The development comes amid a legal challenge to President Donald Trump’s proposal to transform the public course into a championship-level golfing destination. Despite earlier indications that construction could begin in September, the administration has yet to publish a final design, a detailed budget or a timeline for closing the facility. The course remains open to golfers.The first phase of the latest operation began on October 10, according to subsequent reporting by the Associated Press. The Park Service maintains that the trees selected for removal do not contribute to the property’s historic landscape and says the work will not change the course’s holes, routing, greens, bunkers or landforms. Officials have also indicated that healthy trees recognised as historic features, including significant cherry trees, will be preserved. The agency has described the operation as an effort to address neglected maintenance and restore the landscape’s historic character. It is also moving ahead with the work independently of any final decision on the proposed redesign, leaving the broader future of the course unresolved.A legal fight over the course’s futureThe tree-cutting comes amid a lawsuit brought by two golfers and the D.C. Preservation League against the Interior Department and the National Park Service. The plaintiffs argue that the proposed redevelopment should undergo the required environmental review and public consultation before work proceeds.The dispute has already reached federal court. U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes previously declined to halt the earlier removals, allowing the government to continue routine maintenance while the case proceeds. The court has nevertheless sought advance notice of significant activity at the site, including the removal of more than 10 trees or the use of large equipment.The government maintains that the current clearing is separate from the proposed transformation. The plaintiffs, however, argue that treating preliminary work as maintenance risks allowing changes to the property before the larger proposal has undergone the necessary scrutiny.Park users raise concerns over public accessThe debate extends beyond the golf course itself. East Potomac Park is used by cyclists, runners, families, anglers and other visitors who value its open recreational spaces. Among the concerns is the future of Ohio Drive, the popular loop around Hains Point that forms part of the area’s appeal for people who do not play golf.As Axios reported in August, park advocates have organised demonstrations and gathered thousands of petition signatures calling for greater transparency around the administration’s plans. Critics fear that a championship-oriented redevelopment could change the character of a facility long used by the wider public.The administration has yet to provide a final design, a confirmed project cost or a comprehensive construction schedule. It has also not clarified what changes, if any, would affect surrounding park users. For now, the immediate tree-clearing operation is moving ahead while the proposed overhaul remains under evaluation. The central dispute is whether the work represents overdue upkeep of a historic public facility or an early step towards a transformation whose full implications have yet to be made public.You use AI every day. articles.title: Hurricane Simon skirts Mexico’s Pacific coast as beachside communities and tourist areas prepare for impacts
articles.summary: Category 4 Hurricane Simon threatened coastal communities and popular tourist destinations along Mexico’s Pacific Coast on Sunday, as authorities urged residents to take shelter.
articles.body: Category 4 Hurricane Simon threatened coastal communities and popular tourist destinations along Mexico’s Pacific Coast on Sunday, as authorities urged residents to take shelter. The international airport in Puerto Vallarta, a resort city on the shore of Bahía de Banderas, suspended operations as the powerful storm moved north-northwest offshore, along the coast of Mexico. After initial models projected that Simon would make landfall on Sunday, the storm changed course and its path is getting harder to predict. It’s now expected to remain offshore through Monday, and the models are split on whether it will actually move inland or stay entirely offshore. The hurricane is moving at a speed of 7 mph with maximum winds of 140 mph, according to the 1 p.m. ET report issued Sunday by the US National Hurricane Center (NHC). The “extremely dangerous” storm is about 85 miles west-northwest of Manzanillo, a coastal city in the Mexican state of Colima, and 65 miles south-southeast of Cabo Corrientes, in the state of Jalisco, according to the NHC report. The national coordinator of Mexico’s Civil Protection Agency (CNPC), Laura Velázquez Alzúa, told reporters that despite the hurricane not yet making landfall, it is still “very close to the Mexican coast.” But authorities are urging residents to take shelter, as the storm’s path is still somewhat uncertain. “We ask that you remain vigilant,” Velázquez said. The coordinator said that the effects of Simon — which include “strong winds, high waves, and storm surge,” particularly along the northern coast of Jalisco state — will continue through Monday. The storm’s current projected path indicates that it has several “probable impacts” on certain states, which is why “Simon concerns us greatly,” Dr. Jorge Zavala, a climate scientist at the National Autonomous University of Mexico, told CNN. Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum urged residents of Jalisco, Colima, Michoacán, and Nayarit to remain in shelter “until an official announcement that the danger has passed” after the CNPC warned of “exceptional rainfall” and “intense winds” in those states. “The wind and rain will suddenly and deceptively subside, creating an apparent calm that does not mean the danger has passed,” the agency warned in a statement. Nonessential activities have been suspended, and precautionary evacuations are continuing, Sheinbaum said on Sunday. Along the boardwalk in Puerto Vallarta, police reminded tourists that the area was closed and urged them to take shelter as the storm approaches, the Associated Press reported. “We don’t know the extent of the danger yet,” visitor Brenda Villareal told the AP. “We’re just starting to see what’s going on.” Mexico’s Navy deployed more than 4,600 personnel to help with the response to the incoming storm, along with excavation equipment, heavy machinery, and other emergency resources. As Simon moves closer to the coast, its heavy rain has already caused damage. Federal authorities are working to restore power in some areas, including Acapulco, a coastal city in Mexico’s Guerrero state that was devastated three years ago by Hurricane Otis. In Manzanillo, the Navy helped remove water from some houses that were flooded by the storm. Manzanillo resident Cecilia Palomar told Reuters that the water started rising in her home at dawn. “It had risen before, but not like this,” Palomar said. “Beds, refrigerators, heaters, all the furniture got wet, the whole house is flooded.” The Pacific Airport Group (GAP) reported that the Puerto Vallarta airport will remain closed until 10 a.m. ET on Monday. Flights at the airport in Manzanillo were also suspended for the day. Uriel Blanco contributed to this report.

articles.title: A retired US Army veteran has spent 11 years hunting Burmese pythons in the Everglades; Florida pays up to $18 an hour, but every catch demands a close encounter
articles.summary: A retired US Army veteran has spent 11 years tracking invasive Burmese pythons through Florida’s Everglades, where a single capture can bring extra pay
articles.body: A retired US Army veteran has spent 11 years tracking invasive Burmese pythons through Florida’s Everglades, where a single capture can bring extra pay but hours of searching may yield nothing. WUSF Public Media reported that the state pays contractors up to $18 an hour for searching on foot, with additional money for each snake caught. Yet the work is far from an easy way to earn a living. Hunters must navigate dense wetlands, handle powerful reptiles at close quarters and follow strict rules for their removal. Their efforts target a growing threat to Florida’s native wildlife.How hunters track invasive pythons through Florida’s wetlandsAycock has spent 11 years hunting Burmese pythons in the Everglades. His work takes him along isolated roads and into wetland areas where the snakes have been spotted before. He divides his time between North Carolina, Florida's Panhandle and Homestead, where he keeps a recreational vehicle while working in South Florida.The conditions can help determine whether a search succeeds. Falling temperatures and moisture collecting on a vehicle's windscreen can signal a change in the night air, which Aycock associates with increased python activity. Rather than rushing through an area, he scans the vegetation and checks places where young snakes might emerge.Burmese pythons can remain difficult to see against the surrounding vegetation, and a hunter may spend hours looking without finding one. Aycock has described going for months without a catch, despite returning repeatedly to familiar areas. Florida does not permit hunters to use firearms to kill the snakes, so capturing them requires close contact. Although Burmese pythons are not venomous, their size, strength and ability to strike make restraint difficult, particularly when a large animal is involved.Why Florida is trying to remove the snakesBurmese pythons are not native to Florida. Established populations in the southern part of the state have become a serious concern for wildlife managers because the snakes prey on a wide range of mammals and other animals. Their spread through the Everglades has been difficult to measure precisely, leaving scientists without a reliable count of the entire population.The US Geological Survey has estimated that tens of thousands of pythons may be present in South Florida. Females can lay dozens of eggs in a single clutch, with an average clutch containing roughly 29 to 50 eggs. That reproductive capacity makes it difficult to control the population through occasional hunts alone.The consequences for native animals have been documented in research. A 2012 study cited by the USGS recorded steep declines in several mammal populations across parts of the Everglades following the establishment of Burmese pythons. Raccoon numbers had fallen by 99.3 per cent, opossums by 98.9% and bobcats by 87.5% compared with earlier levels.Contractors are paid by the hour and by the snakeFlorida's python removal programme offers contractors a way to earn money while helping wildlife authorities tackle the problem. The state has employed contractors to search for the snakes throughout the year since 2017, through a programme involving the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission and the South Florida Water Management District.The payment structure combines hourly rates with a fee for each animal caught. Under the rates reported by the Associated Press in August 2024, contractors received $13 an hour while driving along back roads and $18 an hour when searching on foot in the wetlands. They could also earn $50 for a python measuring up to four feet, followed by another $25 for each additional foot.The arrangement rewards successful catches but does not guarantee a steady income. Hours spent searching do not necessarily produce a snake, and the work can involve repeated trips through the same areas. Aycock has been clear about the financial limitations, describing the earnings as supplementary rather than enough to support someone working at it full-time.By the end of 2023, more than 18,000 Burmese pythons had been removed from the wild through Florida's efforts, according to figures reported by the Associated Press. Contractors accounted for about 11,000 of those removals.The Florida Python Challenge brings in hundreds of huntersThe state's annual Florida Python Challenge offers another route for members of the public to take part in the removal effort. The event is designed to encourage people to search for invasive snakes over a limited period, while drawing attention to the ecological damage they can cause.Aycock takes part in the competition each year. In 2024, more than 600 hunters entered the 10-day event, which concluded on 18 August. Participants competed to remove as many pythons as possible, with a $10,000 grand prize for the person who humanely killed the highest number under the competition's rules.Catching a python requires a different approach each timeThere is no single method that works in every encounter. Some hunters use a snake hook to control an animal before restraining it, while others rely on their hands when the python appears calm enough to handle. Experienced hunters also learn to recognise signs that a snake may be nearby, from its position in the vegetation to the smell they associate with its presence.Tom Rahill, founder of the Swamp Apes, a veterans' therapy organisation involved in invasive snake removal and environmental work, is among those who hunt alongside Aycock. Rahill has spent years in the wetlands and says familiarity with the terrain helps him judge when conditions might favour a successful search.Even experienced hunters can face a difficult struggle when they encounter a large python. Aycock recalled capturing one measuring 17 feet, or around five metres. He and his wife had to manoeuvre around the animal before he could secure its head and prevent it from lunging at them.A second person can be essential when restraining a large snake. The animal must be kept under control until it can be secured, and hunters need to ensure it cannot escape during transport. Their work involves more than spotting a snake and lifting it from the grass.What happens after a snake is caughtOnce a python has been captured, the contractor must follow Florida's rules for handling and delivery. The snakes have to be handed over to the wildlife agency within 24 hours, and transporting a live invasive snake is restricted to licensed contractors.Aycock takes the animals home before euthanising them with a captive bolt, a method used to kill the snake. The process is part of the requirement that captured pythons be humanely killed rather than released elsewhere.For someone who likes snakes, this is the hardest part of the job. Aycock has spoken about his reluctance to kill the animals, even while recognising the environmental reasons for removing them. His work is directed at the damage caused by an invasive population, rather than a general dislike of the species.Long stretches without a catch are part of the workDuring the Associated Press team's visit in August 2024, he continued looking well past midnight without finding a python. The group eventually stopped for the night, only for Rahill to spot a hatchling about an hour later.Such outcomes are familiar to people who work in the Everglades. A night of searching may yield nothing, even when hunters know the habitat and have spent years learning where the snakes are likely to hide. On other occasions, a brief glimpse in the grass can lead to a catch.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: El-Sayed asked if he believes America is 'ready for a Muslim president' ahead of Senate race
articles.summary: Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed deflected questions about a presidential run, insisting his focus remains on winning the Michigan Senate race.
articles.body: Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed remarked on whether he would consider running for president of the United States, during an interview on NBC's "Meet the Press" Sunday. Host Kristen Welker closed her interview asking El-Sayed whether he believed America was "ready" to elect a Muslim candidate for president. "That's not a question I'm asking," El-Sayed answered. "I think Michigan is ready for a Muslim senator." MICHIGAN DEM HOPEFUL ABDUL EL-SAYED JABS CNN GIVING HIM 'NON-CONSENSUAL COLONOSCOPY' IN RECENT INTERVIEWS Welker repeated the question, but El-Sayed continued to say the question was "irrelevant" and that Michigan was ready for a Muslim senator. "Okay, but you don't rule out the possibility that—?" Welker asked. "I have no intention of ever running for president. That is not a thing I've ever wanted to do," El-Sayed said. EL-SAYED TAUNTS TRUMP, CLAIMS HE'S GOING TO MAKE HIM 'MAIN CHARACTER OF THE MIDTERMS' He continued, "I want to be a really great senator for my state. You know, someday, somewhere, somebody down the line decides to run, that would have been a really amazing thing to see how big America really is. But for right now, I really want to be the next senator from Michigan. That's what I’d like to be for a long time to come. I'm looking forward to serving out the next six years. I'm honored to get to do this. And look, America is a big place, and America has this incredible way of reminding us how big she really is. And that starts in Michigan." During the interview, Welker also asked another question about a presidential run while referencing a reported comment made by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., where she remarked, "If Abdul can win in Michigan, anybody can win anywhere." HARRIS JOINS FORCES WITH RADICAL SENATE NOMINEE IN KEY SWING STATE AS 2028 WHISPERS SWIRL "If you lose Michigan, does that mean that a progressive like AOC can't win the White House in 2028?" Welker said. "Look, this is one seat in Michigan that has a lot more to do with our local issues in Michigan than it has to do with a national referendum," El-Sayed said. Fox News Digital reached out to NBC and El-Sayed's campaign for comment. El-Sayed's interview came after his Thursday debate with GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers in which Rogers brought up alleged ties between El-Sayed and the Muslim Brotherhood terrorist organization. El-Sayed has repeatedly denied these ties. He also rejected the premise when asked by Welker. "No," he said, before claiming the allegation was based in Islamophobia. "It's truly shameful, but he has no ideas, he doesn't actually care about solving problems," El-Sayed said of Rogers. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In a comment to Fox News Digital, Media Research Center President David Bozell criticized what he considered Welker's eagerness to consider El-Sayed a presidential candidate. "NBC took one look at Abdul El-Sayed and started planning the presidential library. Never mind Hasan Piker. Never mind Michigan. Meet the Press skipped the vetting and went straight to measuring El-Sayed’s Oval Office drapes," Bozell said.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: An IndiGo flight from Delhi to Chennai Sunday was diverted to Hyderabad after a passenger's personal electronic device caught fire.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: An IndiGo flight from Delhi to Chennai Sunday was diverted to Hyderabad after a passenger's personal electronic device caught fire. The crew put the device in water before the aircraft safely diverted to Hyderabad."6E 6115 was diverted to Hyderabad after smoke was detected from a customer's PED. Cabin crew responded promptly and the situation was brought under control. In line with established protocols, the pilots diverted the flight and landed safely at Hyderabad," an IndiGo spokesperson said.The personal electronic device (PED), containing a Li-ion battery, or power bank that caught fire was kept in overhead baggage.Many countries, including India, mandate that such devices be kept in front of passengers so they can quickly spot if they start emitting smoke or catch fire. The idea is to avoid delays.However, despite announcements, passengers ignore this instruction and keep power banks or portable electronic devices in bags placed in overhead bins.The biggest concern remains airlines taking cabin bags from passengers at boarding gates to be kept in the aircraft's baggage hold. These bags may contain PEDs and power banks, and a fire in the belly baggage hold may go undetected.The civil aviation ministry is aware of the issue and is working to resolve it."Another aircraft has been arranged to continue the journey to Chennai. articles.title: US Homeland Security secretary sees no ‘risk’ from livestreamed execution
articles.summary: Decision to livestream Nidal Hasan execution has led to harsh criticism and warnings that it could encourage violence.
articles.body:
United States Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has defended the planned livestreaming of Nidal Hasan’s execution, playing down warnings that images of his death by firing squad might be used as a propaganda tool for violent groups.

In an interview on Sunday with the CBS News show Face the Nation, Mullin framed the decision as part of President Donald Trump’s hardline approach to crime.

“I follow President Trump. He’s a commander-in chief of the country,” Mullin said, crediting the Republican leader with “restoring America values”.

Mullin also brushed aside concerns that the images of Hasan’s execution could be leveraged against the US.

“I don’t see an elevated risk at this point at all because of this,” Mullin said. “I think people need to understand, if you attack America, we will come after you, and we will make sure that the punishment fits the crime.”

Hasan, a former US Army major, was sentenced to death in August 2013 after being convicted of shooting and killing 12 unarmed active-duty soldiers and a retired serviceman at the Fort Hood military base in Texas.

The attack took place on November 5, 2009, when Hasan opened fire in a medical facility on the base where service members receive routine check-ups before deployment. The incident is considered one of the deadliest mass shootings to take place on a US military base.

Another 32 people were injured in the shooting. In the process of responding to the attack, police on the military base shot Hasan, leaving him paralysed from the waist down.

Critics have questioned the optics of broadcasting a firing squad killing of a man in a wheelchair. The livestreamed execution is scheduled for December 3.

But Mullin dismissed those concerns, arguing that viewership is optional. “Once again, no one has to watch it if they don’t choose to,” Mullin said.

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth had announced plans last week to livestream the upcoming execution, triggering a wave of criticism. But Trump on Saturday suggested he may reconsider the decision.

“There are two thoughts: Don’t show it and show it. Because, you know, by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did,” Trump told reporters outside the White House.

“So I’ll make a decision, ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we’ll make a decision.”

Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, however, have denounced the idea of a public execution.

In a Sunday morning appearance on NBC’s Meet the Press, Republican Senator Thom Tillis warned that broadcasting Hasan’s death would “put at risk” US lives.

“Terrorist organisations will use this as a recruiting tool. It will radicalise other people, and this is not who we are,” Tillis said.

“Look, the Fort Hood shooter should be put to death, but there’s a way to deal with this that’s proper, and there’s a way to deal with this that’s more improper than I have ever observed in my life.”

Tillis, whose term as senator ends in January, also directed criticism at Hegseth for what he suggested was reckless leadership.

“It’s another example of why Pete Hegseth and all of his bravado needs to get the hell out of the Department of Defense, because he is a failed leader,” Tillis said.

The senator was considered one of the deciding votes in Hegseth’s January 2025 confirmation vote, and he has since called his support for Hegseth’s cabinet nomination “the biggest regret” of his tenure.

Other Republicans echoed Tillis’s concerns about the livestream. Senator Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, for instance, compared the public execution with something she would expect “from terrorists and dictators”.

She also argued that Hasan has sought public attention, something he would receive in a broadcast execution.

“It would give this individual, who deserves no further notoriety, the martyrdom he seeks,” Murkowski added.

Republican Representative Tom Barrett of Michigan, a former military member, issued a statement on Friday explaining that he had trained at Fort Hood a year before the attack.

He also said he opposed the public execution, despite considering Hasan “evil”.

“Secretary Hegseth should seriously reconsider this decision,” Barrett wrote on X .

“Making a public spectacle out of an already tragic situation is unnecessary and does not serve a public interest.”

Military executions are extremely rare in the US and can only be approved by the president under the Uniform Code of Military Justice.

If the order against Hasan is carried out, he will be the first member of the US military to be executed since 1961.

articles.title: Debt advice that may leave you owing even more money
articles.summary: People are increasingly falling behind on credit card repayments, so here's the best way to get debt advice.
articles.body:
An increasing number of people are missing credit card repayments as finances are stretched by rising bills.

Lenders have told the Bank of England they expect the number of unpaid credit card debts to keep going up this autumn.

This could lead to more demand for advice on how to deal with debts – but, if you are struggling and need help, there are some traps to avoid.

And it is worth remembering that impartial advice is available free of charge from debt charities. So here's what to think about.

If you find yourself with money troubles, it can be tempting to seize any opportunity to get things back on track.

Social media and internet search pages are full of supposed quick-fix debt solutions. Cold calls and WhatsApp messages also promise debt help.

But they may well come with upfront fees, unrealistic claims about writing off debt, and pressure to make a quick decision.

Suggestions on the best way to find help include:

Impartial, authorised debt advice comes free. You can find a provider on the government-backed Moneyhelper website

Check whether a firm offering debt help is authorised by the regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). You should cross-check the authorisation details they give with the FCA's register

Anyone unhappy with the service from an authorised firm can complain and, if you are still not happy, go to the independent Financial Ombudsman Service.

Alison Walters, director of consumer finance at the FCA, said: "Anyone struggling with debt deserves advice that puts their interests first.

"Free, impartial debt advice is available to everyone, and no one should be pressured or misled into paying for a debt solution that may not be right for them."

The FCA says that some unregulated firms collect people's details, through cold calling or online adverts, sometimes impersonating debt advice charities or debt collectors, and pass this information on to firms offering debt solutions that you pay for.

A quick search online will throw up lots of businesses offering ways to clear your debt, not all of which are trustworthy, according to charities.

Warning signs of unscrupulous firms include pressure tactics, such as repeated contact, often in messages and on the phone, pushing people to agree to a debt solution, the FCA says.

Some people have been encouraged to change financial details on lenders' paperwork, or are "coached" in ways to respond.

Sometimes people are steered towards a fee-charging debt solution, such as Individual Voluntary Arrangements (IVAs) or some debt management plans, without alternative options being properly explained or offered first.

And, do you know who you are talking to? Ask them who they work for, and check if their details match the firm's official details.

"Before making any decisions around how to deal with your debts, it's always worth getting full, free and impartial debt advice first, exploring all options to clear your debt in the safest and most sustainable way," said Vikki Brownridge, chief executive at debt charity StepChange.

articles.body: Indian high commissioner to Canada, Dinesh Patnaik, has said India doesn't mind advocacy and protests for Khalistan, as long as these are peaceful. articles.title: Powderfinger: Iconic Australian band announce first tour in 17 years
articles.summary: The band, who announced their reunion last week, say they are "absolutely ecstatic" to be playing together again.
articles.body:
Powderfinger, one of Australia's best loved rock bands, has unveiled details of a comeback tour – to take place 17 years after they broke up.

The Brisbane-based group, who confirmed their reunion last week, will kick off with four nights in their home city next September.

They will then play another 14 shows across Cairns, Sydney, Adelaide, Perth and Melbourne, with all gigs to be staged in a "stadium sized big-top" tent.

In a statement on Monday the band said they were "absolutely ecstatic" to be getting together and playing again.

"Over the years there have been tons of suggestions for us to go back on the road but, until now, it never felt quite right or lined up for all of us," they said.

"We have always been so grateful for the continued support from our long-term fans and over the years we've picked up a lot of new ones who have never seen us play."

"People often tell us that our music is connected to their most treasured and joyous memories," they added. "We hope to spread a little more of that joy when we make our way around the country with some of Australia's best established and upcoming talent, and to make some new memories for us all."

The tour schedule of only playing on Friday and Saturday nights is similar to that adopted by Oasis in their world tour last year. No gigs outside of Australia have yet been announced.

Powderfinger released seven studio albums during their career including 2000's Odyssey Number Five which was voted best Australian album of all time by listeners of Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) music station Triple J in 2011.

That included the single My Happiness, which was voted sixth in the 100 best Australian song of all time by the same station in 2025. The group's other hits include On My Mind and These Days and Sunsets.

Since the band split, frontman Bernard Fanning has maintained a solo career while bassist John Collins has gone on to open two of Brisbane's largest live music venues.
